thread.title: Semaglutide Weight Loss: 20% Reduction in New Study
thread.title_full: Semaglutide Weight Loss: 20% Reduction in New Study

author: Grace Chen
title: Semaglutide Weight Loss: 20% Reduction in New Study
text:
Higher Dose of Semaglutide Substantially Boosts Weight Loss, New Trials Show
A new analysis of two large clinical trials reveals that a higher weekly dose of semaglutide (7.2 mg) can drive significantly greater weight loss and metabolic improvements in adults wiht obesity, including those with type 2 diabetes.
A more potent dose of the popular weight loss drug, semaglutide, is showing promising results in clinical trials, offering a potential breakthrough for individuals struggling with obesity and related metabolic conditions. The findings, published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology on September 14, 2025, suggest that a 7.2 mg weekly dose substantially outperforms the currently approved 2.4 mg dosage.
STEP UP Trials: Investigating a Higher Dose
The research centers around the STEP UP and STEP UP T2D trials,the first of their kind to specifically investigate the safety and effectiveness of increasing the semaglutide dose for weight reduction. Participants in these international, phase 3 trials were randomly assigned to receive either the higher 7.2 mg dose, the standard 2.4 mg dose,or a placebo over a period of 72 weeks. Importantly, all participants also received guidance on lifestyle modifications, including dietary support and increased physical activity.
Dramatic Weight Loss Results
The results were striking.In participants without diabetes, those treated with the 7.2 mg dose experienced an average weight loss of nearly 19%, significantly exceeding the 16% reduction observed with the 2.4 mg dose and the mere 4% reduction seen in the placebo group. Remarkably, almost half of those on the higher dose lost at least 20% of their body weight, with roughly one-third achieving a reduction of 25% or more.
For individuals with obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D),the higher dose yielded an average weight loss of 13%,compared to 10% with 2.4 mg and 3.9% with the placebo. alongside this weight loss,participants experienced meaningful reductions in blood sugar levels and waist circumference.
Metabolic Improvements Beyond Weight Loss
The benefits extended beyond simply shedding pounds. participants on the 7.2 mg dose also recorded improvements in key health markers, including waist size, blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels – all factors closely linked to the risks associated with obesity.
Safety Profile remains Favorable
According to the study authors, the higher dose of semaglutide was generally well-tolerated. The most common side effects were gastrointestinal in nature, such as nausea and diarrhea, and some participants reported sensory symptoms like tingling. However, these side effects were largely manageable, tended to resolve over time, and did not lead to a notable number of participants dropping out of the trials.Notably, there was no observed increase in serious adverse events or severe hypoglycemia with the higher dose.
Implications and Future Research
These findings suggest that a higher dose of semaglutide could represent an vital new treatment option for individuals who have not achieved satisfactory results with current therapies. “By delivering greater weight reduction and metabolic benefits while maintaining a favorable safety profile, this higher dose could help more people reach their health goals and reduce the burden of obesity-related complications worldwide,” a senior official stated.
However, researchers emphasize the need for further inquiry to fully understand the long-term benefits and risks associated with the 7.2 mg dose. Continued monitoring and research will be crucial to optimize treatment strategies and ensure the safety and efficacy of this promising new approach.
Reference: “Once-weekly semaglutide 7·2 mg in adults with obesity (STEP UP): a randomised, controlled, phase 3b trial” by Sean Wharton, Paula Freitas, Jøran Hjelmesæth, Maria Kabisch, Kristian Kandler, ildiko Lingvay, Maria Quiroga, Julio Rosenstock and W Timothy Garvey, 14 September 2025, The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. DOI: 10.1016/S2213-8587(25)00226-8.
